approachQuestion.prompt:
Trimmed label

A lowercase string s is a label. Delete exactly k characters without reordering the survivors. Return the lexicographically smallest surviving string. Lexicographic order uses a<…<z; every candidate has the same length n-k.

Example 1: s="cbacd", k=2 → "acd".
Example 2: s="aaaa", k=2 → "aa".
Example 3: s="z", k=1 → "".

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 0 ≤ k ≤ n. The returned string is a new result value; the input remains unchanged. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Scan characters with a separate stack buffer and a remaining-deletions counter. While deletions remain and the top character is greater than the current character, pop it and spend one deletion. Push the current character. After the scan, remove any remaining required deletions from the end. Copy the surviving buffer into the returned string.
options.feedback: At the first differing position, replacing an earlier larger character by an available smaller one improves lexicographic order. Popping only while the deletion budget allows preserves feasibility. Equal characters need not be popped; if no improving pop remains, removing the suffix preserves the smallest prefix.

options.text: Delete the k largest characters by value, breaking ties by deleting the latest positions.
options.feedback: A late large character can matter less than an earlier smaller one. For s="bacz" and k=1, deleting z gives "bac", while deleting b gives the smaller "acz".

options.text: Sort the characters and return the smallest n-k characters.
options.feedback: Sorting does not preserve survivor order. For s="ba" and k=0, the only legal result is "ba", not "ab".

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method. The separate stack is a preallocated n-character array with a top index; each push or pop takes constant time. After scanning and trimming, copy the surviving characters to a new returned string. Count the separate stack buffer even though the returned string is excluded. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair, where n=len(s).
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

options.text: Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)

feedback.reason: Every character is pushed/popped once before copying the surviving buffer.

messages.text: The specified method stores a linear array.
No scan restarts for each position.
There is no sorting or logarithmic search.

details: Each character is pushed once and popped at most once, so total stack work is O(n), even though a single character may trigger many pops. The final copy costs at most O(n). The separate n-character buffer takes O(n) auxiliary space; the new returned string is excluded. No recursion or hashing is used.
Preallocated n-character stack, constant-time push/pop, aggregate worst-case scan; final output copy counted in time and excluded from auxiliary space.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(1)”: The specified method stores a linear array.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(n)”: No scan restarts for each position.
“Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)”: There is no sorting or logarithmic search.
